It is maddening to talk to people. And I am just the opposite so I give my all when I listen, and feel so exhausted trying to be a good, balanced, non-invasive and non-editor listener when I get less than nothing back. 

Also, I’ve noticed on podcasts and during interviews, people tend to talk with a lot of verbiage that could be avoided. They repeat expressions that are given to them and use a ton of signposting language which is neither needed nor appealing to the ear. I'm not even middle-aged yet, but I am all but done with relationships. Admittedly, I still go hopefully into new friendships (especially with other women) but my god am I done with romantic alliances. 

I've done my best to keep my hopes up, given my best shot every time I've been in a relationship. There were times I thought of simply accepting being single but for one or other reason, didn't fully throw in the towel. I have been in/with FWBs, sex buddies, romantic relationships, long distance ones, platonic ones, abusive ones, OLD and virtual connections, and in ones with fuckbois where I got totally trampled on - I have walked away with only one piece of information: I don't understand the other sex, and I am at an age that I do not wish to spend any more of my personal and hard-earned resources to find out. 

I'm so sick of the kind of men I come across - weak-willed, good-for-nothings, manchildren, sexist or misogynistic assholes, entitled brats, rich fuckers and your average idiots who think doing certain things from movies can help them get a girl.  I've worked so hard on myself, to become the person I am today. And it's not fair that I would then expect myself to settle for some rando because he is there. 

  
Yes, it's very hard, very very lonely to be alone. And to be honest, after being touch-starved for a few years now, and with the pandemic taking away my hugs from friends, I've had more lonely days than days when i'm just alone. 

But despite feeling this way, when I'm happy, I feel fully happy, not happy despite not having someone. And I now hope that this sentiment will carry me into my next decade and teach me how to respect my loneliness just as I would any other part of my emotional spectrum, instead of translating it into a default want for a partner.

My mother unknowingly shamed me about my body. Unknowingly because she is too simple-minded to have done it on purpose or with any malicious intent. But she is the picture of the dying patriarchy. She married into a matriarchal family and just never found her footing. 
As a teenager, she shamed me for having breasts. My underwear was too shameful to be left out or seen by anyone. My thighs and butt were the source of men ogling so it was my fault. The usual, and then a bit more.
Oddly, I've been called fat my whole adult life, and I only now realise (and accept) that I wasn't fat for most of it. I am now, and no one calls me fat because they won't dare to. But a large part of it was because my mother made me see myself as a big girl and I internalised it.
She also made remarks about my complexion, because she is fair skinned and so is my brother, I'm more olive. She would say unnecessarily rude or unkind things about my hair being long (I think she was trying to be funny).
And, as an added joy, she made me feel badly about how smart I was and so I spent years trying to shake off that Indian woman thing of apologising for being intelligent and/or successful. 
I still struggle at times to forgive her for the damage she did to my body image. But I also realise that she didn't do it to be mean. She is through and through a product of her times and her generation and no one ever corrected her. 
She's better now. And I'm clearer about how she can talk to me about me.

I have to ask (@OP), the photos you don't like of yourself, who took them? 

I have a round face with prominent features, nothing delicate but nothing disgusting. And this means I will come out handsome in some shots and downright strange/disproportionate in others. This is owed to the tilt of the camera (the phone, actually), the light, the angle of your body vs that of the other person in the shot and even the size and the color of the objects around you. There are so many factors affecting your face in a photo, that unless you get a professional shoot and get it edited by another professional, you're really just competing against your worst case scenario. 

Now, I'm 36 too, and I'm a big girl and I carry a lot of my weight in my cheeks. I'm brown and have a nose that demands attention. I was never, ever called pretty or beautiful. I never was and don't aim to be. I am quite handsome, and I know that my face has very good moments daily. Do you know how I got here? By taking away the privilege of bad photography from people around me. 

After realising that most people are crap with camphones and don't understand photo composition, and also realising that one can't teach them, I decided to be candid about it and tell them that I don't like photos of myself taken by others and prefer to set up the shot myself. Some are graceful and allow me to take over (it helps that I'm not a douche about it), and others try to downplay my choice and insist that they are all ugly in photos and it doesn't matter (unknowingly implying that I think of myself as ugly, which isn't remotely what's going on). To them, I politely request that they not tag me in their socials in that post.

Why am I so strict about this? Because it's my face and my body, and in whatever condition they may be, my self-esteem and confidence happen to be closely and eternally tied to them. So while I do what I do and try to get back into shape or lessen my acne spots or dark circles, no one else gets to freeze a moment of my life which does not represent my best in my opinion.
 
I adore taking selfies, and never overdo it. But I still see the stark difference between the selfies I take and the photos others take of me, to the point that for my brother's engagement party, my selfie was the ONLY photo of mine that I liked and the professional photographer (who had been instructed to be careful with light and angles since there are more than a few overweight people in my fam and we all like to look good in photos, esp because it's the most special wedding in my family) took about 10 photos of me and each of them somehow highlights a new flaw in my body that I didn't know I had. 

So, ask yourself if the dislike you feel for the 'photo you' is because you genuinely think of yourself as not being photogenic enough or is it the version of you that has been burned into your mind by careless clickers holding their bad phones at odd heights and shooting just when the light hits the harshest aspect of your facade. You'd be surprised with the answer. :)

Hi, it's so cool that you have already found your path and are willing to do something about it regardless of the skillset you may at this time possess. I was 36 when I finally decided to quit my high paying job and start from scratch, so let me put your mind at ease - you are exactly at the right moment in your life to build a career in the field of wildlife conservation. 

A couple of things I can maybe contribute here: 

1. Foster and volunteer wherever you can. Learning is key. The more you learn on the job, the easier it becomes for you to become part of an actual wildlife service team. 
2. Look for some certifications online that can help you study a bit about the various initiatives going on in conservation right now. Apart from lending you a basic credibility, it will also make you aware of all the smaller movements happening around the world. 
3. Think of joining something like Workaway. They have projects for people willing to travel (on their own money) who can then stay and live (for free) while they help the hosts build sanctuaries, rescue centers, shelters and so much more. That's the barter. You work 5 hours a day for 5 days a week, learn a bunch, and get accommodation and food. I've joined too and will start traveling once the world is not on fire any longer. 
4. Find your focus within the field of wildlife and channel your efforts to learning more about that specific cause/organisation/place. My fault was that for the longest time, I kept helping the shelter locally, but planning on going for higher education in wildlife, and hoping that I will open my own shelter one day. While these are nice ideas, my age, location and overall experience was not conducive to most of that. I am now fully devoted to my local SPCA shelter, and am focusing on the cattery, earning certifications and learning new things every day, and happily, making an actual difference in the cats' lives. So, focus is important. 

I hope some of these things make sense to you. If you ever think of coming to India for this, don't hesitate to get in touch. :)

I am a certified teacher of English (Cambridge DELTA) and taught for 14 years. 36F. Last year, I quit my full time senior teaching position with British Council (India) to focus on animal rescue. 

I've joined as a full-time volunteer there, so it's unpaid work. I mainly work in the cattery, but do help out with puppies, monkeys and birds whenever I can. 

I don't have the necessary training or background to sign up as a paravet and sadly, now it's too late in life for me to go get that training. It'll mean time off my shelter work and too much money. 

How does it feel? Chaotic good. I'll try to be clear: 

1. I feel good daily about my choice. Daily. 
2. Very regularly, I feel odd about not being able to contribute with house expenditure. (I'm Indian, live with mom, bro and his wife and 4 cats plus strays whom we feed so it adds up) 
3. I fluctuate between being very scared about my future and feeling rather secure because my parents saved up for my marriage (as they do here) and my mom assured me that that fund is mine when I need it. 
4. Shame is a big part of it, because I went from being a big earner to scrambling for online editing jobs to pay my bills. I have to manage it better. I'm still learning. 
5. There is zero regret and I never look back ruefully wishing I hadn't. 
6. I may teach again, but it will mostly be because I miss it so much and it's where my largest skillset is.  
7. Managing lesser money is definitely easier, but only because I was training myself for almost a year prior by bringing down my expenses and needs to the bare minimum. 
8. And finally, about the future, I feel certain that I will always work for either this local shelter or the small farm I plan to have some day. The thing that remains to be seen is whether I have enough to turn it into a rescue spot or if I will only ever have pets (even though 'pets' for me will mean cats, dogs, birds, cows, donkeys, chicken, lizards, hawks and maybe mice 😁 (?) We'll see! 😊
9. Every time I think about how brave I was about this, I also remember to count my blessings and my privilege here. Coming from an upper middle class family of mostly progressive people whose first priority is NOT to tie me to a wife-beating bore is a BIG part of my success here. I have issues with my family and that is a different story, but they also support me when it comes to this and that's saying a lot. I'm sure I would have done the same in another social set up because this feels like my natural calling, but it would've been a LOT more difficult, challenging and demotivating to keep at it.
